reviews.title: LinkedIn- Where careers are Displayed. Opportunities stay behind Glass doors
reviews.text:
An impressive shop window. A disappointing job search experience.

LinkedIn excels at showcasing professional success. Personal branding, company promotions and carefully curated career stories all have a prominent place. What feels far less convincing is its ability to connect people seeking work with meaningful employment opportunities.

In my own experience, and among the people around me, I have not seen the hiring outcomes that would justify its reputation as an essential recruitment platform. There are plenty of vacancies on display, but the experience often feels like window shopping: everything is visible, yet little feels genuinely accessible.

I recognise its value as a marketing and visibility tool. But visibility is not the same as opportunity, and submitting applications is not the same as making progress.

For a platform so closely associated with careers, the gap between displaying opportunities and helping people access them deserves serious attention. I would like to see greater hiring transparency, clearer application outcomes and more accountability around job listings.

A professional network should help people move forward—not simply give them a better stage on which to describe where they already are.

LinkedIn restricted my account, required me to verify my identity using my passport through Persona, accepted the verification and still kept my account restricted without clearly explaining what I supposedly did wrong.

For a company that presents itself as the world’s leading professional networking platform, this is shockingly poor. If you restrict someone’s account after asking for sensitive identity documents, the bare minimum should be a clear reason, a transparent review process and access to a real human being.

What is especially alarming is seeing multiple users recently reporting the exact same pattern: sudden restrictions, completed identity verification, rejected appeals and no real access to human support. At that point, this does not look like an isolated mistake it looks like a serious systemic failure. For a platform handling professional identities and sensitive documents, that is completely unacceptable

Automated restrictions, automated responses, and practically inaccessible human support is not a serious security system. It is a broken process. Deeply disappointing and far below the standard expected from LinkedIn.

Now the kicker is that I got logged out of my account on the app and LinkedIn is asking me to confirm it's me by sharing a code that they sent me... on the app... makes absolutely no sense and I can't log back it... but having recently changed jobs, it also made me realize that I really didn't need to endure the aforementioned annoyances in my daily life and that it wasn't worth the hassle of speaking with someone to fix the issue. reviews.title: Less career app & more targeted spam advertising
reviews.text:
It’s difficult to truly write how awful LinkedIn has become over the years but we’ll try giving it a shot.

Firstly, the over the top performative posts by people for everyday elements is quite laughable. Yet this app pretty much survives by promoting this. Is it social media or is it a career app? Not sure we really needed more Facebook style features. 

Secondly, direct messages which are just adverts… who thought this was a good idea? Seriously, this is actually scary that this was an active decision someone made. Privacy is clearly something that went to the bottom of the priority list over ad revenue. No one will appreciate messages from ads.

The jobs board is quite chaotic, it’s meant to be curated based on your experience and activity yet in practice falls drastically short of being remotely relevant. 

Lastly, premium…… I’m sure many would recognise the absurdity of the price tag for the very minimal additional benefits. Use of AI, ability to see which user has decided to check you out (but only if they allow someone to know in the first place) and 1/2 extra potential jobs which inevitably end up being the same as the standard job board. 

Only you get a nice little AI prompt saying you’re a top applicant. 

It feels like it’s time for rival to step in a d offer an experience that fixes everything that LinkedIn is constantly getting wrong.

LinkedIn closed my account because of a job description that was generated using LinkedIn’s own integrated AI tool.

I’m not asking for special treatment. I simply want someone at LinkedIn to review the case and give me back access to my account.

What makes this particularly frustrating is that there appears to be no accessible customer service phone number, no responsive email support, and no way to speak to an actual person. I’m essentially locked out of a platform that I’ve used professionally, with no practical way to resolve the issue.

LinkedIn’s own help pages say that users can appeal account restrictions and that LinkedIn will review them. But in my case, months have passed without a response.

Six months is not a reasonable amount of time to wait for an account review.

I just want my account back. If anyone at LinkedIn can help escalate this to a human being, I would genuinely appreciate it.

reviews.title: Diminishing returns
reviews.text:
Linkedin was invaluable to the job search in 2016. Now, in 2026, this is pretty unrecognizable. AI features are a mess, human Support is impossible to reach. There are no formatting tools for profile editing so importing information is laborious and requires a lot of manual adjustment. The timeline feed is irrelevant. I don’t need Facebook replicated on this app. LinkedIn also does not comply with state laws regarding job salary transparency. Salaries for jobs in states with this posting requirement are often not included and it appears that LinkedIn isn’t doing its due diligence to ensure compliance. Profile views by prospective employers are controlled by 2 pay to play devices- forced engagement within the social media feeds, and paying for Premium. Premium is also a mess. What it seems to reliably do is block the IDs of employers who are monitoring employee profiles. I have not gained any better job matches or functional profile edits by having Premium. 
UPDATE: the developer feedback was not helpful. My issue has been in queue for a human to look at since I posted this review. Their support bots aren’t doing anything about the scam recruiters that I have reported for using fake jobs for phishing scams. The reports are coming back almost immediately with the decision that the scammers aren’t violating TOS. In queue for a human to respond to this too.

reviews.title: Should support preferred name
reviews.text:
LinkedIn should support a clear and safe way to manage identity names.

Many international users use an English preferred name that is different from their legal ID name. The app should allow users to store both a legal name (for verification) and a preferred/display name, with the ability to choose which one is publicly shown.

The current UX is extremely frustrating. After changing my display name, the app logged me out immediately without any clear explanation, warning, or rollback option. There was no notice about what would happen, no confirmation step, and no timeframe provided.

As a result, my account was locked while my display name no longer matched my ID name, creating unnecessary stress and the risk of losing access to a professional account.

This experience feels unsafe for users who rely on LinkedIn for work. A professional platform should provide transparency, clear messaging, and better control over identity settings — especially for global users.

reviews.text: How is it that an app built from the ground up expressly for text posts deletes everything you’ve drafted after you leave, NOT CLOSE, the app for 10 seconds? Make it make sense. No auto-saving, nothing? I just lost at least an hour of writing over this. If you like scrolling through vapid conversations between AI industry “thought leaders” and other pseudo-adults regurgitating their brainless takes about management culture, then this app is for you. If you enjoy receiving career updates from people you have neither seen in 10 years nor care about in the least, despite the fact you are not connections with each other, than this app for you. If, however, you have better things to do with your time than wade through the worst parts of workplace speak distilled into venomous sludge, just to parse out an aphorism easily locatable in an airport self-help book, then maybe back out of this page, say hello to a loved one, and breathe sweet fresh air. Know that social media apps profit as much from your anger as from your joy. Just keep scrolling, just keep scrolling, just keep scrolling….

reviews.title: LinkedIn Premium – Not Worth the Money in My Experience
reviews.text:
I subscribed to LinkedIn Premium with the expectation that it would improve my job search experience. Unfortunately, after trying multiple approaches—optimizing my profile, applying through recommended roles, using InMail, and following the platform’s suggestions—I did not receive a single interview call or relevant job offer.

For me, the Premium features did not translate into any real value, despite paying for a full year. The platform feels ineffective for serious job seekers, and the return on investment has been quite disappointing.

This is my personal experience, and I hope LinkedIn reviews the effectiveness of its Premium job-seeking features so users can get genuine results and value for their money.

reviews.title: Worst and rude customer support
reviews.text:
I’ve been a loyal LinkedIn user since 2020, but my recent experience with their support team has been extremely disappointing. My verified account — which was verified through a government-issued ID — was compromised after my password was stolen. The hacker changed all my account information, including the verified email, and all subsequent alerts were sent to the unauthorized user instead of me.

When I reached out to LinkedIn Support for help, I was expecting a fair review and some understanding of my situation. Instead, I received a response from Prakash, a LinkedIn Trust and Consumer Support Consultant, who was dismissive and unhelpful. I was simply told that their decision was final and that no further correspondence would be made — without any real investigation or attempt to understand my case.

It’s extremely frustrating to see such a lack of care and accountability from a platform that promotes professionalism and trust. I truly expected better from LinkedIn’s customer support team. A loyal user since 2020 deserves at least a fair review, not a template reply and closed ticket.
